evals.prompt:
I want to build a wiki around machine learning concepts for my research. I have some papers and articles I'll be feeding over time.

For now, let's start with this first source:

---
The Transformer architecture, introduced in "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017), represents a fundamental shift in how we process sequential data. Unlike recurrent neural networks (RNNs) that process tokens one at a time, Transformers use self-attention mechanisms to compute representations of input and output simultaneously.

The core innovation is multi-head attention, which allows the model to attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. Each head learns a different set of attention weights, enabling parallel processing of diverse contextual relationships.

Key components include: positional encoding (since self-attention is permutation-invariant), layer normalization for stable training, and a feed-forward network applied identically to each position.

Transformers have since become the dominant architecture across NLP, computer vision (ViT), and increasingly multimodal applications.

---

Please create a new Twillm vault at /tmp/eval-vault-new/ and ingest this source material as tiddlers. Save the final vault state to that directory.
evals.expected_output: A scaffolded vault directory with CLAUDE.md schema, index.md, log.md, and at least 3-4 content tiddlers (e.g., Transformer, Self-Attention, Multi-Head Attention, Positional Encoding). Tiddlers should have proper YAML frontmatter with title, tags, timestamps. Wikilinks between related tiddlers. Source tiddler created.

evals.prompt:
I already have a Twillm vault set up at /tmp/mock-vault-exists/vault with some notes on attention mechanisms and the Transformer architecture.

Here's a new article I'd like to add:

---
Mixture of Experts (MoE) is a technique where the model partitions its hidden units into separate groups called "experts" and dynamically selects which experts to use for each input. This allows the model to scale up parameters without proportionally increasing computation.

In Sparse MoE, only the top-k experts (typically k=1 or 2) are activated per token. A trainable routing network determines which experts to call. Recent large models like Mixtral 8x7B and GShard use this approach to achieve billions of parameters while maintaining tractable inference costs.

MoE introduces new challenges: load balancing (ensuring all experts get used), expert capacity (each expert has a max token limit), and auxiliary loss (to encourage balanced routing). The key benefit is that MoE models can train with the same batch size as dense models while having 10-100x more parameters.

---

Please ingest this into my existing vault at /tmp/mock-vault-exists/vault, linking to relevant existing tiddlers. Modify the vault in place.
